hints: Undo the natural logarithm in \(\ln(1+e^{-3x})=2\) by exponentiating both sides.
Take logarithms again to solve for \(x\), then round only the resulting value to 3 decimal places.
walkthrough:
Exponentiate both sides with base $\mathrm{e}$ to remove the natural logarithm:
$$\mathrm{e}^{\ln(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-3x})} = \mathrm{e}^2$$
$$1 + \mathrm{e}^{-3x} = \mathrm{e}^2$$

Subtract $1$ from both sides to isolate the exponential term $\mathrm{e}^{-3x}$:
$$\mathrm{e}^{-3x} = \mathrm{e}^2 - 1$$

Take the natural logarithm of both sides:
$$\ln(\mathrm{e}^{-3x}) = \ln(\mathrm{e}^2 - 1)$$
$$-3x = \ln(\mathrm{e}^2 - 1)$$

Divide by $-3$ to solve explicitly for $x$:
$$x = -\dfrac{1}{3}\ln(\mathrm{e}^2 - 1)$$

Round the answer to $3$ decimal places:
$$x = -0.618$$
